documentation.range:
This species is widespread across large areas of Europe, though only sporadic or limited in some countries (e.g. the UK and Ireland, Iberia, Scandinavia, the east and southeast). It is well known as a pest and generally considered invasive, and is clearly spreading within these areas.

Its native range is uncertain. It was originally thought to be from Iberia but genetic studies have suggested this is unlikely (e.g. Quinteiro et al. 2005). It may even be native to much of Central Europe, though not in the peripheral areas mentioned above (Pfenninger et al. 2014). Data from several sources has been used to delineate the map which remains approximate (including Bank et al. 2007, Welter-Schultes et al. 2012, Pfenninger et al. 2014, Rowson et al. 2014). In Iberia it has been said to be absent, but it is likely it has not yet been reliably distinguished where it occurs (perhaps as an introduction) given the past confusion with other species. Sampling in Iberia has to date been focused upon the northern coast (Castillejo 1998, Pfenninger et al. 2014). In the Balkans it is thought to be introduced (Wiktor 1996).

This species has not yet been reliably reported from outside Europe, although there are reports from Algeria`that need confirmation (Wiktor 1996).

See taxonomic notes for the potential confusion with A. lusitanicus Mabille, and other species.
documentation.population: There are no total population size data for this species and they cannot reliably be estimated. It is often conspicuously common at a site. The species is expanding its range so the population size is therefore assumed to be stable or increasing.
documentation.habitats: This omnivorous, but mainly herbivorous, species is most common in cultivated and disturbed habitats of all kinds.
documentation.threats: This species is not considered threatened at a European level, nor at any national level. There is some evidence for hybridisation with other species in areas to which it has been introduced (e.g. Dreijers et al. 2013, Rowson et al. 2014) but this is unlikely to threaten A. vulgaris as much as the other parent species involved.
documentation.measures: There are no especial conservation measures for this species. It does not appear on any regional Red Lists.
documentation.use_trade: This species is not used or traded.
documentation.rationale:
Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)
EU 28 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)

This species is widespread across large areas of Europe, though only sporadic or limited in some countries (e.g. the UK and Ireland, Iberia, Scandinavia, the east and southeast). It is well known as a pest and generally considered invasive, and is clearly spreading within these areas. Records outside Europe, from Algeria, require confirmation. Although more remains to be learnt about the precise past and present range of this species, it is clearly expanding in several areas and the population is increasing. It is therefore listed as Least Concern (LC).
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
It is important to note that this widespread pest species has been, and still is, incorrectly called A. lusitanicus Mabille, 1868 or "A. lusitanicus auctt. non Mabille, 1868" (e.g. Dreijers et al. 2013). This account does not concern the true A. lusitanicus Mabille which is restricted to Portugal (Castillejo 1998, Quinteiro et al. 2005, Welter-Schultes 2012, Dreijers et al. 2013, Pfenninger et al. 2014, Rowson et al. 2014). Systematic and nomenclatural works by several authors are ongoing (e.g. R. Bank pers. comm. 2015).

This species is a member of a group of large Arion species which have often been confused with one another, and sometimes require dissection for successful identification. The species include A. ater (Linnaeus, 1758); A. rufus (Linnaeus, 1758); A. vulgaris Moquin-Tandon, 1855 (=lusitanicus auctt. non Mabille); A. lusitanicus Mabille, 1868; A. flagellus Collinge, 1893 and others.
